title: Fire alarm in a training centre
audience: Trainee: rescuer or junior officer on duty
context: Educational, non-combat civil-protection scenario. No weapons, harm or combat content.

steps.title: The alarm sounds
steps.situation: You are presenting to 14 participants in a second-floor training room when a continuous alarm begins to sound. Nobody has announced a drill and nothing in the room looks wrong. Several people look at you.
steps.question: What do you do first?

options.text: Tell everyone it is probably a test and carry on while you check.
Stop the session, tell everyone to leave now and lead them to the exit.
Ask people to stay seated until someone confirms what the alarm means.

steps.why: The guide says to treat every alarm as real until it is officially confirmed otherwise, so the group leaves at once.
steps.hint: Think about what the sound of an alarm can and cannot tell you.

steps.title: It is probably a test

Agree it is likely a test, but ask everyone to be ready to go.
Send one person to reception to ask while the group waits.

steps.why: A test and a real alarm sound the same, so only an official confirmation can change how you treat the alarm.
steps.hint: Ask who is entitled to decide that an alarm is not real.

chat.question: How should the burn be treated later?

chat.answer: The guide uses 112 or the local emergency number.

chat.question: Why point at one specific person?
chat.answer: A general request makes everyone assume someone else has already called. Naming one person, and asking them to report back, makes sure the call actually happens.

chat.question: Why not stop and call myself?
chat.answer: Stopping pressure on a severe bleed lets it start again. Keep pressing and delegate the call.

chat.question: What should the caller say?
chat.answer: Give the location, what happened, the number of injured people and any hazards, then stay on the line until told to hang up.

steps.title: Assembly point
steps.situation: You and your colleague, with pressure still applied, reach the assembly point. The headcount shows that one person from your group is missing. Paramedics arrive.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: Go back inside to look for the missing person.
Wait quietly until someone asks you.
Tell responders the missing person's name and last known location, then hand over the casualty: what happened, what you did and when.

steps.why: Clear information to responders is the fastest way to help the missing person and the casualty.
steps.hint: Responders need specific facts about anyone missing. Think about what to pass on, and to whom.

chat.question: Why is the assembly point away from the entrances?
chat.answer: The guide places it away from the building and its entrances so emergency teams can get in and work without people in their way.

chat.question: Why not go back in to look?
chat.answer: The guide says not to re-enter the building until responders declare it safe. The fastest help for the missing person is giving responders their name and last known location.

chat.question: What goes into a good handover?
chat.answer: A short, ordered handover: what happened, what you found, what you did and when, and any changes since. Name any missing person and the last place they were seen.

chat.question: Why not send someone else in?
chat.answer: Sending someone back in puts another person at risk and gives responders a second person to look for. Leave the search to them.

steps.title: A cool door
steps.situation: With pressure still applied, you and your colleague reach the bottom of the south stairwell. A shut door leads to the ground-floor lobby and the exit. You check it with the back of your hand: it is cool.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: Open it slowly, ready to close it at once if you see smoke or feel heat.
Open it wide and send everyone through at a run.
Leave it shut and take the group back upstairs to look for another route.

steps.why: A cool door can be opened, but slowly and with care, so you can shut it again if there is smoke or heat behind it.
steps.hint: Think about checking what is behind a closed door before the group commits to it.

chat.answer: Even a cool door can hide smoke. Opening it wide leaves no chance to shut it again, and running in a group causes falls. The guide says to open a cool door slowly, ready to close it at once.

chat.answer: A cool door means the route may be usable. Going back up takes everyone away from the exit and back towards the smoke.

steps.title: The missing person
